en: 2. Regarding the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*):
This realm is so named because its material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), consisting of both the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya* and *upabhoga*), are preeminent;
it is named after this excellence. It is also generally termed the "Brahma World" (*brahmaloka*); "Brahma" carries the meaning of purity, as it is free from the defilement of desire.
Therefore, because they are born of dhyāna and because they differ from distracted movement, this realm contains eighteen heavens in total.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The three dhyānas each have three [levels], and the fourth dhyāna has eight," which excludes the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is the same as the present sutra, with the addition of "non-perception.
The text has three parts:
first, a general indication.
"Ānanda! Among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, if they do not rely upon *dhyāna*, they will possess no wisdom.

This passage generally clarifies that those who cultivate the mind must rely on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) before wisdom can arise; when concentration and wisdom are balanced, it is termed "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). If this is not the case, it cannot be called *dhyāna*. This intends to reveal that within these four stages, both concentration and wisdom are essential causes.

However, because there are differences in the degree to which the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within them have been suppressed, the various heavens are distinguished; this will be explained in detail below.

Alternatively, this passage may refer to worldly persons who do not cultivate untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) and do not give rise to untainted right wisdom (*anāsrava-samyag-prajñā*), thereby experiencing the retribution of the four dhyānas but being unable to achieve liberation.

Although ordinary beings are said to practice dhyāna, it is merely the six types of outflowing (sāsrava) contemplation; as their objective observation does not transcend delusion, it is not called *dhyāna*. As the subsequent text states:

"These three superior streams, though not the correct cultivation of true samādhi," and again: "They are merely able to restrain the body and refrain from sexual desire," and further, the concluding summary says: "All these arise from the accumulation of delusions within the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; through delusion, the three realms come into being. Etc.
2. Detailed Explanation, in four parts:
1. First Dhyāna, in two parts:
1. Explanation, in three parts:
First, the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*Brahmapāriṣadya*).

"Those who are able to maintain their bodies without engaging in sexual desire—whether walking or sitting—being entirely free of such thoughts, in whom no defilement of attachment arises, and who do not remain within the realm of desire: these people, by virtue of their mindfulness, should consider themselves companions of Brahmā."
"Such a class [of beings] is called the Brahmakāyika devas.
Because their minds are focused exclusively on this, it is said that they "are only able to maintain the body," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "devoid of both thought and recollection": by practicing the six modes of conduct, they cultivate revulsion toward the lower desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, while they aspire to the higher form realm as being pure, subtle, and detached; thus, the afflictions of the desire realm are suppressed, which is termed the non-arising of craving and defilement.
Because one passes away from this state and is immediately reborn in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), it is said that there is no lingering in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
This is precisely the non-arising of coarse suffering and the manifestation of pure signs; it is thus "pure concentration" (śuddha-samādhi).

Those born from savoring this [meditative state] are called the Brahma-pāriṣadyas (Brahma’s Retinue); they are the result of the subduing of afflictions through the six practices cultivated by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Second, the Brahmapurohitas (Brahma’s Ministers).

“When the habit of desire has been eliminated and the mind free from desire manifests, one takes delight in and accords with all forms of discipline; such a person is able to practice the virtue of Brahma at that time.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma.”
Having already subdued the afflictions of desire, it is said that "the habituation to desire has been eliminated.
Having attained the first dhyāna, the concentrated mind becomes manifest; thus, it is said that "the mind free from desire appears."
This concludes the section on the [Brahma]kāyika devas.

Regarding the section below on the [Brahma]purohita devas: it correctly clarifies that these devas delight in and accord with the *samādhi-saṃvara* (precepts associated with meditative concentration), thereby accomplishing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), guarding against what is non-virtuous, and remaining without transgression. Thus, they concurrently protect the *vinaya-saṃvara* (restraint of the discipline) and perfect the virtues of pure precepts; because they assist the Lord of Brahmā, they are named Brahmapurohita (Ministers of Brahmā).
Third, the Great Brahma Heaven:

"With body and mind wondrously perfect, majestic deportment unceasing, and pure observance of precepts augmented by clear awakening, such a person is able, at the appropriate time, to preside over the Brahma host as the Great Brahma King."
"Such a class of beings is called Mahābrahmā.
Because their meditative contemplation has become increasingly superior and their rebirth is subtle and refined, it is said that their body and mind are wondrously perfect.
Furthermore, because they possess the virtue of the precepts, it is said that their majestic deportment is without deficiency.
This concludes the preceding section.

From "Pure" (*viśuddha*) onwards, it correctly clarifies that this deity, having given rise to the clarity of wisdom within meditative discipline, possesses an understanding that surpasses others; thus, he is able to serve as the Lord of Brahmā (*Brahmādhipati*), presiding over the assembly of Brahmās.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is said: "His majestic radiance shines alone; he dwells without vitarka and vicāra, being moved by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the two lower heavens possess both vitarka and vicāra."
Furthermore, at the end of a kalpa things depart, and at the beginning of a kalpa they come; failing to discern this, non-Buddhists cling to it as being permanent.
Moreover, because they give rise to the thought that they see the heavens being born, they cling to the idea of a creator who produces the world as the sole causal lord.
2. Conclusion: "Ānanda!

These three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction. Although they do not constitute the true, correct Samādhi, because the various outflows (āsravas) remain unmoved within their pure minds, this is called the First Dhyāna."
Having already departed from the eight sufferings of the desire realm, it is said that they cannot be oppressed by them.
However, because this merely suppresses afflictions through the six practices, it is called "not the true samādhi.

Generally, one who truly cultivates dhyāna does not manifest body or mind within the three realms; even if superior and wondrous signs of concentration appear before them, they clearly know them for what they are and remain free from attachment.

Although one has now attained this semblance of samādhi that appears pure, because it is not fully understood, one becomes attached to its flavor and is reborn; nevertheless, because one is able to leave behind the coarse agitation of the desirous and distracted mind, it is said that "the outflows are unmoving."
Therefore, the commentary concludes: "These three superior flows are collectively termed the First Dhyāna. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion is free from the defilements and evils of the desire realm, and gives rise to the bliss of attained pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)."
Now, the merits attained in this first dhyāna consist of five factors (pañcāṅga): first, applied thought (vitarka); second, sustained thought (vicāra);

third, joy (prīti); fourth, bliss (sukha); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā). Their characteristics are as described in the *Tiantai Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm of Tiantai).
2. The Second Dhyāna has two parts:
first, the explanation, which has three sections;
the first is the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhadeva).

“Ānanda! Next, there is the Brahmā Heaven, where the Brahmās exercise sovereign control, perfecting their Brahma-conduct; with minds clarified and unmoving, they give rise to light from profound stillness.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).”
The King acts as the Lord of Brahmā; therefore, it is said he "governs and encompasses.
He is endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom; therefore, it is said his "brahma-conduct is perfected.
This concludes the preceding section.

Below the phrase "clarifying the mind" (*chengxin*), this passage precisely clarifies that the concentrated mind of this heaven is increasingly superior; thus it says, "the clarified mind is unmoving.
Because the light of concentration radiates forth, it says, "tranquil stillness gives rise to light."

From the second dhyāna upward, because of the departure from vitarka and vicāra, there is no speech; rather, light is emitted by means of the concentrated mind, and their respective stages are distinguished by the superiority or inferiority of that light.
When these devas first arise, their marks of joy are manifest, yet their light of wisdom is still inferior; thus they are called the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābhā*).
Second is the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābhā*).
Their radiance shines forth in mutual brilliance, illuminating without end, reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions until they are entirely transformed into lapis lazuli.
"Those of this class are called the Gods of Immeasurable Light.
From the previous Gods of Limited Light, they emit even more light; because the characteristics of their light increase further, they are called the Gods of Increasing Light (Ābhāsvara).

The radiance of its marks is perfectly bright, reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions; as the environment follows the light to become pure, it becomes entirely composed of lapis lazuli. Because meditative concentration gradually increases, the light of this concentration emits illumination that is necessarily boundless; thus it is named "Immeasurable Light."
Third, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Heaven of Radiant Sound).
"Absorbing and sustaining the perfect radiance, they accomplish the essence of the teaching; their transformative manifestations are pure, and their applications are inexhaustible.
This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
It absorbs and sustains immeasurable pure light, which serves as the medium for verbal expression; this is termed the "body of the teaching" (*śāsana*).
Because this light expresses and signifies that which is free from all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), it is said to "emanate and transform purity."
His spontaneous teachings were always perfectly clear; thus it is said that his applications are inexhaustible.

Because the realm and stage of the second dhyāna lack the first five consciousnesses, they employ light as their means of expression. Taking light for sound, it is called the Heaven of Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara).
2. Conclusion: "Ānanda!

These three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any sorrow; although they do not constitute the true, correct Samādhi, because coarse outflows have already been subdued within the pure mind, this is called the Second Dhyāna."
The three heavens of the second dhyāna are superior to the lower stages; therefore, they are called "the superior stream" (viśeṣa-gati).
Because one attains supreme joy, it is said that one cannot be oppressed by any sorrow.

Although the first dhyāna attains the factor of joy (*prīti*), because extreme joy has not yet arisen and it remains coarse within the body, one merely attains freedom from suffering; there still exists the mutual opposition of sorrow and joy.

Now, in this second dhyāna, the water of meditative concentration moistens the mind, the light of wisdom is serene and expansive, and the factor of joy is perfectly harmonized so that sorrow does not arise; therefore, it is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*).

Regarding "the coarse outflows having been subdued": to rejoice in what is superior and feel aversion for what is inferior is termed merely "subduing"; because they have not been severed, it is not called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
However, this stage possesses a forest of four factors:
first, internal purity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind; their modes of activity are as usual.
3. The Three Dhyānas, Part Two:
1. Explanation, Part Three:
1. Parīttābha (Limited Radiance) Heaven.

“Ānanda! Thus, these devas and humans have perfected their radiant light into sound; they unveil the sublime by opening this sound, giving rise to refined practice, and attaining the bliss of tranquil extinction.
This class is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha).”
The first two phrases refer back to what preceded.

"Pī" (披) is pronounced as in the second tone; this correctly clarifies that this deity—namely, the *pī*—reveals the essence of the teaching (*abhidheya*) through its expressive medium (*abhidhāna*), manifests the subtle principle that is expressed, and accomplishes the sublime practice to be performed.

Thus, once these three types of wisdom have arisen, sublime bliss is thoroughly attained; concentration and wisdom surpass those of the previous stage, and the auxiliary factors become increasingly superior.

Regarding what is called "the bliss of cessation" (*śānta-sukha*): having extinguished the preceding signs of joy, one gives rise to pure bliss. Because the signs of joy are coarse and agitated, this is a bliss of karmic maturation (*vipāka-sukha*) that is tranquil, serene, and still; therefore, it is termed "cessation."
Because the characteristics of meditative concentration are still inferior, it is called a "penetration" (abhijñā).
Having first attained this bliss, which has not yet become extensive and pervasive, it is called "Limited Purity" (parītta-śubha).
"Purity" (śubha) also implies "stillness" (śānta); thus, there is also a heaven named "Limited Stillness" (parītta-śānta).
2. The Gods of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubhā devāḥ*).
When the pure emptiness manifests before them, it induces boundless physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), resulting in the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Gods of Immeasurable Purity.
"Purity and emptiness" refers to tranquil bliss (*śānta-sukha*).
As the concentrated mind becomes increasingly superior, it induces this bliss until it becomes boundless.
Only when the bliss is boundless does it truly fulfill the meaning of "pure bliss"; this is what is called the bliss that penetrates the stage of the mind (*manobhūmi-sukha*).
The pervasive physical pliancy is called "Immeasurable Purity.
Third is the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
"World, body, and mind are all perfectly pure; the accomplishment of pure virtues brings forth a supreme reliance, leading to the bliss of quiescent extinction."
"Such a class is called the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
Although previously they had thoroughly attained the bliss of the mental stage, it was limited to body and mind and thus not yet termed 'universal.

Now, however, it pervades both the primary and secondary [receptacle] worlds; bliss and purity are perfectly interfused, such that there is no place—whether world, body, or mind—not pervaded by this sublime and wondrous bliss, which constitutes their pure virtue."

Regarding the term "supreme reliance," this refers to this very purity and bliss; it is the supreme locus upon which that practitioner relies, and because one realizes this bliss, it is called a "refuge.
Second, the conclusion.
“Ānanda! These three superior streams possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are at peace, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although this is not the true, correct Samādhi, within a state of tranquility, joy is fully present; it is called the Third Dhyāna.”
Regarding "possessing great conformity" (*anuloma*): first, it is conformity with superior meditative concentration; second, it is being free from sorrow and joy.
Since sorrow and joy are both objects of aversion when compared to pleasure, they are merely discordant states and therefore not conformities.

Now, this sublime bliss is the foremost in the world, and there is nothing superior to it; this alone constitutes the meaning of being "conformable and complete. Regarding the phrase "in a mind of tranquility, joy is fully present":

this refers to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) where maturation (*vipāka*) is conformable and sovereign. Bliss reaches its ultimate limit here; being purely singular and without admixture, it is called "fully present" (*paripūrṇa*). For this reason, the third dhyāna is termed the "ground of sublime bliss free from joy."
The meditative factors (*dhyānāṅga*) of this stage consist of five types:
first, equanimity (*upekṣā*); second, mindfulness (*smṛti*); third, wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
Fourth, regarding the four dhyānas: however, the karma that constitutes the general retribution for this single stage consists of only three grades, which induce rebirth in the [lower] three heavens.
The Heaven of No Perception (asaṃjñisattva) is merely a distinct retribution within the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala); it represents the upper limit of the realm of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).

As for the five types of Non-returners (anāgāmin), they are noble ones (ārya) who, having cultivated meditative absorption (dhyāna) in a mixed manner, utilize the karma of the Heaven of Vast Fruit to make their five grades of practice particularly sublime. They are born in those five heavens solely within the body of the general retribution of the Heaven of Vast Fruit, which distinguishes them from ordinary beings.
From this point downward, it constitutes a separate section.
The text has two parts:
first, the four roots; second: [subdivided into]...
1. Explanation, in four parts:
First, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven.
"Ānanda!..."
Furthermore, gods and humans are no longer oppressed by body or mind; the causes of suffering have been exhausted. Pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably decay after a long time.
Both the minds of suffering and pleasure are simultaneously and suddenly relinquished; the characteristics of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.
"Such a class [of beings] is called the Puṇyaprasava devas.
The first five phrases conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The fourth dhyāna is free from eight calamities, namely: vitarka, vicāra, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, as well as inhalation and exhalation."
Furthermore, it is called the "Immovable Ground" because it cannot be shaken by the three calamities.
What is now termed "not oppressed" refers to being free from the suffering of the lower stages.
The subsequent section on suffering explains the reason why one is not oppressed.
Vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), daurmanasya (mental distress), and prīti (joy) are causes of suffering; since these have now been abandoned, there is no longer any oppression.

As for the statement that "pleasure is not permanent," this specifically clarifies the factor of pleasure in contrast to the preceding suffering. Although in the third dhyāna one attains a pleasure that thoroughly pervades the mental sphere, it is nonetheless not permanent and must eventually perish. This perishing constitutes suffering, which is termed *vipariṇāma-duḥkha* (the suffering of change).

Regarding "suffering and pleasure" below: this correctly clarifies that in this heaven of the fourth dhyāna, both suffering and pleasure are abandoned. This is because each respective stage involves a distaste for the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower levels, while taking joy in the purity, subtlety, and detachment of the higher levels.

The abandonment of the suffering and pleasure of the lower realms is called the cessation of the characteristics of *dausthulya* (coarseness); the attainment of the meditative concentration of the higher stages is called the arising of the nature of pure merit. Because this dhyāna-samādhi consists solely of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is the very essence of this merit.
Having already departed from the defilements of the lower realms, it is therefore called "Pure Merit.
Second, the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*).
"With a perfectly integrated mind of equanimity and pure resolute conviction, amidst unobstructed merit, one attains wondrous compliance that extends to the furthest reaches of the future."
This class of beings is called the Puṇyaprasavā devas.

When the single feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) is perfectly integrated with a concentrated mind, one abandons all phenomena such as pleasure and pain; yet, within that state of equanimity, one still gives rise to resolute conviction (adhimokṣa). By being certain, accepting, and maintaining this conviction, one is not led astray by other conditions; therefore, it is called "purity of resolute conviction" (adhimukti-pariśuddhi).

By the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one takes delight in and accords with this perfectly integrated, sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*), causing this sublime concentration to become free from obstruction, such that the mind dwells in mastery and its enjoyment is inexhaustible; therefore, it is said that "one attains wondrous accord that extends to the end of the future," and so forth.
Question:
Since this impure dhyāna has a limited lifespan, how can it reach the end of the future?
Answer:

This refers to the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its resultant longevity, which lasts for many kalpas and is said to extend to the end of the future; it does not refer to what is discussed regarding the state after that retribution has ended.

Furthermore, although this wholesome concentration is still with outflows (*sāsrava*), it can accord with sublime practice: by relying on the fourth dhyāna to induce this concentration, one perfumes the untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna and cultivates the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), and the concentration of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
The five lower types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) also rely on this meditative absorption to practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, alternating between the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
If an ordinary person attains it but does not further cultivate it, their lifespan is permitted to be limited;
if a noble one (*ārya*) cultivates it, they attain [the state] that lasts until the end of the future.
Pervading these two directions, both ordinary beings and sages practice together.
Third, the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
"Ānanda!..."
From this heaven, there are two diverging paths:
if one dwells in the cultivation and realization of the previously mentioned immeasurable pure light and the perfect clarity of merit, such a class is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
Within the pursuit of merit and affection, there are two directions:
first, the direct path, which leads to the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala);
second, the circuitous path, which leads to the Realm of Non-conception (Āsaṃjñika).
This is the heading; it will be explained below.

If, from the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one has not harbored heterodox views but has directly cultivated the fundamental four dhyānas and the four immeasurables, thereby perfuming the merit of dhyāna, becoming free from the defilements of the lower stages, and passing through all four levels until reaching this "Merit-Love" (Puṇyaprasava) and further superior concentration, then through the influence of such vast merit, one attains birth in a superior realm called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
Fourth, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).

"If, in a prior state of mind, one simultaneously feels weary of both suffering and pleasure, and through the diligent cultivation of a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), maintains it in uninterrupted succession until the path of equanimity is fully perfected, then body and mind both cease; the mental faculties become ashen and solidified, lasting for five hundred kalpas."
This is the correct elucidation.

If one is accompanied by heterodox views, one subdues afflictions through the six practices, gradually becoming weary of and abandoning them, until reaching the Heaven of Merit-Love where equanimity becomes perfectly integrated.
With this continuity of the mind of equanimity, one thoroughly exhausts the path of equanimity.

The mind of equanimity also perishes, and one no longer reckons with body or mind; therefore, it is called "the simultaneous extinction. This reckoning of non-conception as nirvana constitutes the use of this mind of equanimity as a skillful means to enter the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).

First, one abandons the coarse mind and enters the subtle mind; then, abandoning the subtle mind, one enters the extremely subtle mind. By constantly practicing from the extremely subtle mind without ceasing, one enters the state of non-conception; these are all the causes of cultivation.

When mental deliberations subside, one enters the state of non-conceptualization; at the end of life, as a karmic fruition, one is born in the Heaven of No-Thought (Āsaṃjñika), where the lifespan lasts for five hundred great kalpas. Because the faculty of thought does not function there, it is called "the solidification of ash."

"Since these people take arising and ceasing as their cause, they cannot manifest the nature that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing; for half an eon they cease, and for the latter half of the eon they arise.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of No-Thought."
This judgment is rendered false.

Failing to realize that the essence of deluded thought is empty, one clings instead to the weariness of arising and ceasing; thus, one detests this arising and ceasing and seeks non-arising and non-ceasing. Therefore it is said: "Taking arising and ceasing as the cause, one abandons the born to pursue the unborn; yet this is not true non-arising."

Seeing that the sixth consciousness does not function for a brief moment—like a fish trapped in ice—one fails to recognize its subtle arising and ceasing, falsely claiming it to be *nirvāṇa*; yet this is not true *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that one cannot manifest the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
The first half-verse below explains the characteristics of that retributive state.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which cites the *Mahāvibhāṣā* to explain the stages of birth and death therein: for a long time one possesses perception; having first been born in this heaven, after the passage of half a kalpa, one finally enters the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-perception, which is termed "extinction after the first half-kalpa."

When the time for their impermanence arrives, they emerge from maturation (*vipāka*) and remain conscious for half an eon (*kalpa*), only dying thereafter; these are called those born in the latter half of the eon.
During the interval between birth and death, they are consistently without perception; thus, they are named the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
2. Conclusion: "Ānanda!

These four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly states of suffering or pleasure. Although they are not the unconditioned stage of true immovability, because the mental effort of those who still possess a 'grasping mind' has reached full maturity, they are called the Four Dhyānas."
"This fourth dhyāna is free from the eight calamities; because it excels the lower stages, it is called the 'Immovable Ground.
However, since there are kalpas [of duration] and one must eventually relinquish it when one's lifespan ends, it is said that it is not truly immovable."
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "However, those receptacles (the physical world) are not eternal, because they arise and perish simultaneously with sentient beings.
When ordinary beings cultivate meditative concentration and become attached to the flavor [of the dhyāna] as they take birth, this is called "having attainment" (*upalambha*).
When concentration and wisdom are balanced and one is able to relinquish both suffering and pleasure, surpassing the lower heavens, this is called the full maturation of spiritual effort (*prayoga*).
Second, the five heavens of the Non-returners (*anāgāmin*); three parts:
first, the general indication.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, there are five types of non-returning devas within this realm. Because the nine grades of habitual tendencies in the lower realms are extinguished simultaneously, both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and they no longer dwell in the lower regions; therefore, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class of equanimity.”
Regarding the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), these refer to the nine grades each within the desire realm and the first, second, and third dhyānas.
When both the seeds and their manifestations are absent, it is termed "complete extinction."
This is called "cessation" because it is the severance [of defilements] by the Noble Ones; it is not the same as the "cessation" of ordinary beings, which refers merely to temporary suppression.

Since habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) no longer exist, both suffering and pleasure are simultaneously extinguished; having departed from the bonds of the lower realms, there is no fixed dwelling place.

However, because they have not yet progressed to severing the afflictions of the fourth dhyāna, a separate dwelling place is established within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the mind of equanimity; this distinct residence exists because, at the time of practicing dhyāna, the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states are intermingled.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Through five distinct grades of mixed cultivation of the dhyānas, one is reborn in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

As for these five distinct grades, they are: the inferior grade, the intermediate grade, the superior grade, the superior-excellent grade, and the superior-supreme grade; their specific characteristics are as explained elsewhere.
2. Explanation of the Characteristics, in five parts:
First, the Heaven of No Affliction (*Avṛha*).
"Ānanda!..."
"When both suffering and pleasure are extinguished, and the minds of contention do not interact—this class of beings is called the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha).

When the minds of suffering and pleasure are extinguished, their opposition perishes; since there is no longer any mutual dependence of form, they are said not to interact. Because they do not interact, there is no affliction.

Initially, the two forms of suffering and pleasure cease and depend upon the mind; when one practices the first stage of mixed cultivation and gradually becomes free from the hindrances of meditative concentration, it is called "Free from Affliction" (Avṛha), for "affliction" (vraṇa) refers precisely to these hindrances.

However, although the lower heavens are also free from suffering and pleasure, they are not called "Free from Affliction" (Avṛha), because ordinary beings merely suppress these states through temporary aversion and attraction rather than permanently severing them.
Here, the name is applied based on their ultimate non-arising; therefore, it receives this designation.
2. The Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).
"When the trigger moves alone and there is no ground for contact, such a class is called the Heaven of No Heat.
*Ji* (trigger) refers to the bolt of a crossbow.
"Guo" (括) refers to the "huan" (筈), the notch at the end of an arrow where the string is received;
all these serve as metaphors for the single mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Because it acts with spontaneous mastery while roaming through the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), it is called "solitary."
Because it does not correspond with either adverse or favorable objects, it is said that "there is no ground for the rubbing together [of opposites].

This heaven, by means of the middle grade of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, possesses a wisdom-function that is pure and void; being entirely free from the hindrances of meditative concentration, one gradually attains coolness, and thus it is named "Without Heat" (Atapa). Second is the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).

"In the worlds of the ten directions, the wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid; there are no further images of dust or any defilements whatsoever. Such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).

Because the single mind of equanimity illuminates the subtle and wonderful, pervading everywhere with perfect clarity and stillness, it is said that 'the wondrous vision is perfectly clear and limpid.'"
The image of dust is an obstruction to wisdom;
the settling of impurities is an obstruction to meditative concentration.

When one cultivates the superior grade of mixed practice and the power of the untainted (anāsrava) becomes manifest, the obstructions to both concentration and wisdom perish; thus, one is able to see with wondrous clarity.
Pervading the worlds of the ten directions with perfect clarity is called Sudarśana (Good Vision).
Fourth, the Sudṛśa Heaven (Good Appearance):
when refined vision manifests before one, forging all things without obstruction—this class of beings is called Sudṛśa.
"Smelting and casting" refers to refining and tempering; molding clay is called "pottery," while melting metal is called "casting.

Since the vision of perfect clarity has already been manifested, the merit of meditative concentration and wisdom becomes even more prominent; thus, one is able to exercise mastery over smelting and casting, manifesting inexhaustibly, which is why it is called "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa).
Fifth, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
"Having reached the ultimate limit of the multitude of forms and exhausted the nature of the nature of form, they enter the boundless; those of this class are called the Akaniṣṭha Heaven."
"Ultimate" (*jiujing*) means to exhaustively investigate to the furthest limit.
"The manifold *ji*" refers to the subtle and minute traces of the manifold of existence (*yǒu*).
This denotes the state where one has departed from non-existence (*wú*) and entered existence, yet the principle (*lǐ*) has not yet taken form.
Now, this single principle exhausts [all things] down to the limit where form and principle have not yet taken shape; hence it is said that it "ultimately reaches the myriad potentialities.
To "exhaust the nature of form" means the essence of nature; it refers to tracing back to the primordial essence of the nature of form.

Regarding the meaning of these two phrases, there are many such precedents; either the preceding phrase exhausts the consciousness that takes form and so forth as its object, while the subsequent phrase exhausts the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which it relies. Upon reaching this limit of the single world-system, one enters the sphere of infinite space; hence it is said, "one enters the boundless."
Because emptiness is also that upon which the great elements depend, it is called the "Ultimate of Form" (Akaniṣṭha).
As Aśvajit asked the Buddha:
"In what state do the natures of the four great elements cease without remainder?"
The Buddha said:
"The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is precisely located in this heaven.
Third, the conclusion on its excellence.
“Ānanda! As for these Non-returner devas, the various kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration; they cannot know or see them.
It is just as in this world where vast wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the holy path are all sustained by Arhats, such that ordinary people of the world cannot see them.”

In Sanskrit this is called *anāgāmin*, which here means "one who does not return. Because this heaven is the dwelling place of those noble ones, it is also called the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*), as it is not an impure residence like that of ordinary worldlings.

Because their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is superior, their environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) is likewise superior; though they both dwell within the world, their respective spheres of experience differ, as can be known from examples.
Third, the conclusion.

“Ānanda! These eighteen heavens are solitary and without companions; they have not yet exhausted the burden of the physical form. From this point downward, they are called the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu).

Because they are purely induced by the wholesome perceptions of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and are free from the objects of sensual desire, they are said to be ‘solitary and without companions.’”
Since there is still the obstruction of form (*rūpa-āvaraṇa*), it is said that they have not yet exhausted the burdens of the physical form.

Third is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These four formless states lack the form resulting from karmic fruition; they consist of an abundance of concentration and a deficiency of wisdom. Disgusted by the obstructions of lower forms, one contemplates infinite space; subsequently, becoming disgusted with the sphere of infinite space and so forth, up to the sphere of nothingness, one takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as ultimate *nirvāṇa*. These four types [of states] distinguish their respective stages.

Although there is no matter resulting from karma (*karmaphala-rūpa*), there is nevertheless matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhiphala-rūpa*) that serves as the support for consciousness; this is what the Mahāyāna teaches regarding the actual existence of a locus.

If the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there is no locus; by way of birth, there are four kinds [of beings] who, through the sense-sphere of homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), cause the continuum of mind and its associates to persist."

As for the statement in other sūtras that there are formless sentient beings who listen to the Dharma from the Buddha and shed tears like rain, this refers to the existence of meditative fruits within the Mahāyāna.
The preceding text also mentions that devas of the formless realm make vows to protect mantras.
The prose section has two parts:
first, the enumeration and explanation, which has two sub-sections;
the first is the explicit explanation of the retribution experienced, which has two parts: [the first part].
First, pointing out the turning of the mind so as not to enter [the path].
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
From within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence, there are again two divergent paths between them."
This is the heading. "Existence" (bhava) refers to form (rūpa), and "summit" (mūrdhan) refers to the ultimate.
Form abiding at this point is called the limit of form (rūpānta).
The two diverging paths are:
first, the path leading out of the three realms, which is traversed by those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment];
second, the path leading into the formless realm, which is trodden by those of fixed nature.

If ordinary beings and non-Buddhists do not enter these five heavens, they instead enter from the two heavens of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) and Non-conception (Asaṃjñin); they are not within the limits traversed by these two.
As he knew within himself:

"If, through the illumination of wisdom within the mind of equanimity, the light of insight becomes perfectly pervasive, one will then transcend the realm of dust, become an Arhat, and enter the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas."
"Such a class as this is called a 'Great Arhat who has turned the mind.
This correctly clarifies the turning of the mind.
Since it occurs within the meditative concentration of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is specifically referred to as "abandoning the mind."

He gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and simultaneously severs the thirty-six categories of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) across the four stages of the upper realms, thereby realizing the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
He then turns his mind toward the Mahāyāna path and does not enter again into the spheres of emptiness (*ākāśa*) or consciousness (*vijñāna*), because he lacks the afflictions of those higher stages.
However, there are varying degrees of depth regarding those who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna; these differences depend solely on the depth of their destruction of delusions.
Such individuals are still *anāgāmins* who delight in wisdom (*prajñā-rata-anāgāmin*); thus, by attaining the perfect penetration of the light of wisdom, they immediately transcend the realm of dust.
II. Distinguishing the Differences among the Classes of Those Who Enter [the Formless Realm], in two parts:
A. Specifically explaining the four heavens, in four sections: 1.
The Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāśānantyāyatana).

"If one abides in a mind of equanimity, achieves the perfection of relinquishing aversion, perceives the body as an obstruction, and dissolves that obstruction to enter emptiness—this class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Space."
The first two phrases refer back to what preceded. There are two types of relinquishment of mind:
first, that of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra); [the second is that of the Desire Realm].
Second, the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*).

If, within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one employs the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to sever the afflictions of the Peak of Existence, thereby dissolving obstructions and entering emptiness, this is the *sukha-vihārin* Anāgāmin; that is, the Śrāvaka of fixed nature.

If one enters the state of emptiness by suppressing afflictions through the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) within the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) or the Unconscious (*asaṃjñin*) realms, this is also called the "mind of equanimity" (*upekṣā-citta*); these are the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is because these two heavens both abide in the mind of equanimity and share the same level (*bhūmi*).

From "Awakening to the body below" onward, the text clearly elucidates that the statement regarding this deity’s "dissolving of obstructions" also applies to the preceding two stages. However, when a practitioner grows weary of and afflicted by material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) as if they were a prison, and their mind desires liberation, they immediately cultivate contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to destroy material phenomena and transcend all forms of matter.
Having extinguished the perception of resistance and not attending to manifold perceptions, one enters the sphere of infinite space.
When the mind is associated with space, it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
2. The Sphere of Consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).

"When all obstructions have dissolved, yet there is neither obstruction nor cessation, and within this state only the *ālayavijñāna* remains together with a subtle portion of the *manas*, such a class of beings is called those who abide in the sphere of consciousness."
The first phrase concludes the preceding state of the sphere of infinite space; the second phrase breaks through that emptiness to enter the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Since even the non-existence that dissolves obstructions has perished, it is said to be "unobstructed and unextinguished. This means that one observes only consciousness in order to dismantle the notion of emptiness.

Regarding the main explanation therein, the reason only the *ālayavijñāna* and the complete *manas* are retained is that these two—the seventh and eighth consciousnesses—mutually depend upon one another; those of fixed nature and those who are ignorant of the Dharma do not realize this at all, and thus they remain in a state of profound obscurity.

"Half-subtle" refers to the sixth consciousness; it retains half of its portion that takes consciousness as its object, while not retaining the portion that takes form and space as its objects, hence it is called "half."
Because this sixth [attainment] involves both form and mind as objects of focus, half [of the previous stage] is retained.

When a practitioner enters this meditative absorption, they become weary of the boundlessness of space; since excessive focusing leads to distraction and can destroy the concentration, one abandons space and turns the mind to focus on consciousness. Because the mind corresponds with the dharma of consciousness, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi).
Third, the Sphere of Nothingness:

"When the perception of form has vanished and the conscious mind is entirely extinguished, all ten directions are silent and utterly devoid of any destination; such a class of beings is called the Sphere of Nothingness."

In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), form is absent while emptiness remains; in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), emptiness is lost while consciousness remains;

both are termed "that which exists. Now, in this state, both emptiness and consciousness are extinguished; thus it is said that "emptiness and form have perished, and the mind of consciousness is utterly ceased. These two phrases first dismantle the three dharmas.
"Throughout the ten directions" below correctly clarifies the characteristics of practice.
"The ten directions" refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Since the objects of perception—such as form, emptiness, consciousness, and the mind—do not exist as anything whatsoever, it is said to be "tranquil."
Since the object of perception (*ālambana*) is stilled, the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*) does not function; thus it is said that there is nowhere to go.

Because the practitioner grows weary of consciousness—given that the consciousnesses of the three times are boundless and that manifold objects lead to distraction which can destroy meditative concentration—they abandon the consciousness as an object and turn the mind toward the dharma of non-existence. When the mind is in correspondence with this dharma of non-existence, it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

However, those who now practice the Mahāyāna often conflate it with this meditative absorption; they claim that simply being unattached to all things, having no mental support and possessing not a single entity, constitutes the Mahāyāna, which is no different from inert emptiness.

Yet, if one does not know how to skillfully realize and penetrate the various stages of dhyāna, and clearly discern the sequence of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) through their successive abandonment and suppression—like a great round mirror reflecting the myriad phenomena without error or deviation—then this is not yet the true cultivation of dhyāna according to the Mahāyāna.
Fourth, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception:

"The nature of consciousness is immovable; through the ultimate investigation of cessation, one proclaims the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible. Thus, it is as if existing yet not existing, as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception."
The first two phrases indicate the essential nature of the basis.
The first phrase provides a dual designation: "the nature of consciousness" indicates the presence of subtle perception (*saṃjñā*), while "immovable" indicates the absence of coarse perception.

The next phrase further explains the meaning of "immovability": whereas in the preceding sphere of nothingness one still employs the mind to investigate exhaustively, thereby causing the consciousness-mind not to take objects as its condition and remaining in correspondence with the dharma of nothingness; [in this stage, that too ceases].
Now, this deva investigates and exhausts the cessation of the mind, subduing it so that it does not move; therefore, it is said, "exhaustively investigating through cessation.

Regarding the phrase "within the non-existent," this correctly explains the mode of activity: because he relies on the place where this consciousness is unmoving, it is said, "within the inexhaustible, he distinguishes it as 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'"; thus, it is said, "he proclaims the nature of exhaustion."
Although cessation is perceived, consciousness remains; therefore, it is said that "if it were exhausted, it would not be exhausted.
Although existence is perceived, it does not arise; therefore, it is said that "it exists as if it did not exist.
For these reasons, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

This refers to the fact that while coarse conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of the sixth consciousness does not arise, subtle discernment (*sūkṣma-vikalpa*) and the continuous flow (*pravāha*) of the ālayavijñāna still persist; therefore, its name is established based on this meaning.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is said: "The first three formless attainments derive their names from their mode of practice (*yathā-prayoga*), whereas this stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is designated according to its essential nature.

When a practitioner enters this meditative absorption, they become weary of the perception of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) as being like delusion, and the sphere of perception (*saṃjñāyatana*) as being like an abscess or a sore; they then abandon the sphere of nothingness and take as their object of contemplation the state that is neither-perceptual-nor-non-perceptual (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Because the mind is associated with these dharmas, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Second, a general analysis of the two categories:

"These [practitioners] exhaust emptiness, yet do not fully realize the principle of emptiness. By extinguishing form and grasping at emptiness, they do not attain the nature of true emptiness; they falsely claim to have reached its end, and thus it is said they "do not exhaust" it, because they are unable to utterly extinguish their mental consciousness.
The phrase "these" refers collectively to the four heavens.
"Those who have reached the ultimate limit of the holy path from the Heaven of No-Return"—such a class is called the dull-witted Arhats who do not turn back their minds.

"Immediately, having achieved the renunciation of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they perceive their bodies as obstructions; dissolving these obstructions, they enter into emptiness. Since they were unable to manifest wisdom and suddenly sever the higher afflictions to achieve the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), they turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle. Thereupon, by means of the untainted noble path, they gradually renounce [the lower realms] through wearying detachment, and according to their meditative concentration, they experience the resulting fruit and are born in these four heavens."
Because they must undergo the retribution of kalpas before severing the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) to become Arhats, they are termed "dull-witted.

As for the phrase "those who do not turn their minds," this is said provisionally in contrast to those of sharp faculties; it does not mean they never turn their minds at all, as has already been explained previously.
"If one follows the non-conceptualizing externalist heavens and exhausts the realm of emptiness without returning, remaining deluded, leaking, and ignorant, one will then enter the cycle of rebirth.

If one proceeds from the state of non-conceptualization by using the path of outflows—rejoicing in what is above and loathing what is below—one gradually reaches the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; mistaking these outflows for the realization of the unconditioned, one then claims it to be Nirvana.

Failing to progress further at this point, because they have not extensively heard the holy teachings and have not discerned the characteristics of the various meditative absorptions—whether tainted or untainted—in their cultivation and realization, they will, upon the end of their lives, necessarily enter the various realms of existence according to their karma.

When it is said that they come from the Realm of Non-conception (asaṃjñika), they must be those coming from the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala), as this shares the same level as the Realm of Non-conception. In contrast to the five noble heavens, they are termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika); because they belong to the class of non-Buddhists, it is said that they come from the Realm of Non-conception.
If one truly enters the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), one will inevitably fall back and no longer advance in cultivation.

According to the exegesis of the sūtras and śāstras, those non-Buddhist practitioners in the realm of non-conception must fall once their karma is exhausted, as there is no principle of higher rebirth for them.
2. Distinguishing between Kings and Ministers: "Ānanda!
These various devas among the heavens are all ordinary beings whose karmic fruits are being requited; once their retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of rebirth."
"That Heavenly King is a Bodhisattva who, through the gradual advancement of his practice in samādhi, has turned toward the path of cultivation followed by the noble assembly.
While the celestial beings of the four heavens of the formless realm may be the result of karmic retribution, that Heavenly King of the Four Great Kings is a provisional manifestation."

This is because, having entered the Mahāyāna Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he desires to sport within the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and all other meditative concentrations (samādhis) in order to accomplish the work of a Buddha.
Question:
Is the previous King of the Four Dhyānas also a provisional transformation, accessible to ordinary beings?
Answer:

The celestial kings of the four dhyānas necessarily include both ordinary beings and noble ones (āryas), as stated in the preceding text: "The five non-returner heavens and the celestial kings of the four dhyānas alone possess reverent hearing [of the Dharma], yet they are unable to know or see it."
"This refers to what is said regarding a portion of ordinary beings; thus, one should know that it includes both [categories].
Second, the conclusion and indication: 'Ānanda!'"

"In these four heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), body and mind are extinguished; the nature of concentration manifests before them, and there is no form resulting from karma. From this point until the end [of that state], it is called the Formless Realm.
As for "body and mind are extinguished": the physical body (*rūpakāya*) necessarily ceases; as for the mind, whether it actually ceases or not, they falsely claim it has ceased.
Regarding "the manifestation of those with fixed natures," there exists matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
If this matter did not exist, upon what would the four types of mind rely?
Therefore, we know it exists.
2. Summary of Falsity:

"All of this arises from the failure to understand the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind, which accumulates delusions and gives rise to them. Thus, there are falsely the three realms; within them, one falsely follows along as one sinks and drifts through the seven destinies, with each *pudgala* following their own kind."

Because one does not know the single Dharma of suchness as it truly is, one falsely identifies what is revealed; once discrimination has arisen, delusion accumulates upon delusion, which is why it is said that "one does not understand," and so forth.

It should be known that when practitioners of dhyāna do not penetrate this gate, they may remain for sixty or eighty thousand great kalpas in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; though their body and mind are in a state of quiescence, when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back down. This is collectively termed the "difficulty of the long-lived heavens."
Since this was personally proclaimed by the Buddha’s own mouth, how could one not believe it with clarity?
*Pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly takes up existence.
Seventh is the realm of *asura*.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
Within these three realms, there are four classes of asuras.

Those who, belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts, enter the air by means of supernatural power through the efficacy of protective dharmas—these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the destiny of hungry ghosts."

If one descends from the celestial realms due to the depletion of merit, and their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon, this asura is born from a womb and is categorized within the human realm.

There is an asura king who upholds the world; his power penetrates all things and he is fearless, able to contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. This asura exists through transformation and is categorized within the realm of the devas.

Ānanda! There is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caves; they roam through the void in the morning and return to their watery abodes in the evening. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also state that there are four types of asuras, which are largely identical to this [explanation].
Various accounts of asuras—whether classifying them as devas or pretas—are all unclear; this scripture is explicit and may serve as the standard.
3. Concluding with the causes of delusion as a warning to abandon them.
This has two parts:
1. Concluding the causes of delusion. This has four sections:
First, a general summary of their falsity: "Ānanda!
Thus it is with those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras"—here he summarizes the various realms of existence.
"Having thoroughly investigated the seven realms of existence, they are all but the delusive signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

Birth is received through false conceptualization, and one follows karma through false conceptualization; within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky, fundamentally without attachment, being merely a single falsehood with no further root or source."
This constitutes the formation of falsehood.
"Thoroughly investigating" means seeking minutely.
"Birth through deluded thought" refers to the fruits of the seven realms of existence.
Deluded thoughts follow karma and serve as the cause for the seven realms of existence.
These deluded causes and effects are all the empty, conditioned marks of ignorance; no reality can be found therein.
If viewed against the perfect luminosity, they are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent. How could any root or trace be found?
2. A general demonstration of the causes of karma: "Ānanda!

These sentient beings do not recognize their original mind; they undergo this saṃsāra, passing through immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity. This demonstrates that birth arises from deluded thoughts.
"All arise from following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
By reversing these three, one further gives rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
This demonstrates how deluded thoughts follow along with karma.
"Named are the realms of ghosts; unnamed are the celestial realms. Through the mutual overturning of existence and non-existence, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
This concludes the cycle of transmigration.
"The realms of ghosts and the celestial realms" briefly cite two of the four evil and three good destinies.
Existence and non-existence depend upon one another, mutually overcoming and displacing each other; rising only to fall again, the wheel of existence has no beginning.
Third, revealing correct practice:

"If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then there is wondrous, eternal stillness. Both existence and non-existence are absent, and even 'non-duality' is extinguished. Since there is not even 'not killing,' 'not stealing,' or 'not committing sexual misconduct,' how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct?"
"If one arouses this samādhi, one sees only the secret treasury of the three virtues as a single essence:
'Wondrous' refers to prajñā;
'Eternal' refers to the dharmakāya."
Quiescence (*śānti*) is liberation.
When both existence and non-existence are absent, it is not saṃsāra.
When even the absence of duality ceases, it is not nirvāṇa.

The single principle of the Middle Way and True Reality (bhūtatathatā) is such that there is no other dharma apart from True Reality; therefore, it is asked: "How could one further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?
Fourth, the specific indication of the final summary.
“Ānanda! If one does not sever the three karmas, each possesses its own private [retribution].
Because of these individual privacies, the collective commonality of these privacies has no lack of a fixed location.”
These arise from one's own delusions; their arising is without cause, and there is nothing to be sought or investigated.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are committed individually by each person; thus they are called "private" acts.
Because that which is produced is identical, it is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Since karma and suffering correspond without any discrepancy, it is called a "fixed location," which refers to the place where [retribution] is experienced.
Since it is called delusion, how could it have a cause?
Therefore, there is nothing to be sought after.

This concludes the answer to the previous inquiry as to whether [the retribution] has a fixed location or arises spontaneously, and how those who initiate karma each privately experience their own results.
2. Exhortation to Eliminate and Sever:
"You must exert yourself in practice; if you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions.
If you do not exhaust the three delusions, even if you should attain supernatural powers, they will all be merely worldly, conditioned functions."

If habitual tendencies are not extinguished, one falls into the path of Māra; though one wishes to eliminate delusions, one instead doubles one's hypocrisy. The Tathāgata calls such a person pitiable: you have created this delusion yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
"To speak thus is called speaking correctly; if one speaks otherwise, it is the speech of Māra.
This is the primary exhortation for those who wish to eliminate the three delusions.
The previous passage stated: "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; the nature of madness naturally subsides, and this subsiding is itself Bodhi," and so forth.
The following section clarifies the fault of non-severance: practicing meditation without upholding the precepts is the work of Māra; to cultivate delusion within delusion is truly pitiable.
You have rashly provided a definitive answer to distinguish between the correct and the erroneous. Your previous question asked:
